title: Zephaniah
subtitle: the day is near, and then God rejoices aloud
lead: Zephaniah is three chapters from Judah's last great reforming king. The prophet, who traces his family four generations back, speaks in the reign of Josiah and begins with a verdict wider than Judah: the LORD will sweep everything off the surface of the ground, people and animals, birds and fish. Then he closes in on Jerusalem, where people bow to the stars on their roofs, swear by the LORD and by Milcom in one breath, wear foreign clothes, and say that the LORD will do neither good nor harm. The day of the LORD is near, with fury, darkness, the ram's horn and the battle cry, and silver and gold cannot buy anyone out.

The book is not only judgment. In the middle comes a quiet call: seek the LORD, you humble of the land, "perhaps you will be hidden." Then the compass swings through the nations: Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush and Assyria. Jerusalem is next, and no better. And at the end the same God who swept the earth gathers the nations to call on his name with pure lips, leaves behind a humble people, and cries out for joy over a rescued Daughter Zion. The book that opens with a warrior shouting in defeat ends with a warrior who rescues, quiet in his love.
facts: Zephaniah son of Cushi, of a family traced four generations back to a Hezekiah (1:1). Nothing else is known of him. Jewish tradition counts the Twelve as one scroll written down by the Men of the Great Assembly (Bava Batra 15a).

In the days of Josiah (640 to 609 BC), says the heading. Most scholars place the prophecy before the reform of 622 BC; some place it later in the reign. Many critics think the closing hope (3:9-20, or some of it) was added in the exile or after.
Jerusalem and Judah under a boy king, with Assyria still the world power and Babylon about to rise
Hebrew poetry, with a prose heading (1:1). Oracles of judgment, a call to repentance, oracles against the nations, a woe on Jerusalem and a shout of joy.
3 chapters, 53 verses (18, 15, 20). English and Hebrew verse numbers agree.

The ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai...) and in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah...).

The Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex. The Greek read here is Swete's text (mainly Codex Vaticanus) via the site's Septuagint printout. The Dead Sea scrolls 4QXII-b (4Q77), 4QXII-c (4Q78), 4QXII-g (4Q82) and the Judean desert scroll Mur88 (MurXII) preserve parts of the book.
authorship: Zephaniah the prophet wrote or spoke the book in Josiah's reign. Jewish tradition counts it as one of the Twelve, written by the Men of the Great Assembly (Bava Batra 15a).

Most critical commentators date a core to Josiah's reign (Berlin, Sweeney) and differ on the rest. Sweeney reads the whole book as a unit composed to support Josiah's reform. Ben Zvi argues that the book is a composition from after the monarchy. Others see exilic or post-exilic additions at 2:8-11 and 3:9-20, because the hope there speaks of a scattered people being gathered and fortunes being turned around. The text of the hard verses (2:1-2; 2:14; 3:1; 3:8; 3:17-18) is a separate question.
Defenders of the book's unity argue that hope after judgment is a regular part of the prophets' pattern and does not need a later author. Kapelrud and Ball study the book as a rhetorical whole.

audience.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah in the early or middle years of Josiah, a king who came to the throne at eight after his father Amon was murdered. The court was run by officials, the Temple still held shrines to other powers, and the empire of Assyria still collected tribute. Most commentators take the oracles against the nations as spoken to Judah, not to the nations themselves.
audience.why: To warn a people who think the LORD will do nothing (1:12) that he is about to act, and to say exactly where: in the royal house, the officials, the priests and prophets, the merchants and the comfortable householders. At the same time to give the humble a way to live: seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility, and perhaps be hidden. For later readers, in exile and after, the book explained why the day had come and promised a gathering. Knowing the audience changes the reading: a sermon preached to the comfortable is not a forecast of the end of the world, even where it uses the language of the end.
views: Josiah's Jerusalem before the reform (about 640 to 622 BC)
The commonest view (Berlin, Sweeney): the book warns Jerusalem while Baal, the idol priests and Milcom are still there, and it supports the reform that follows.
Ben Zvi and others: the book was shaped for a post-monarchic community, to explain the fall and offer hope. The Josiah heading is then part of the book's literary setting.
A Josianic core with later hope
Many critics: the warnings are Zephaniah's, and a later hand added the hope of 3:9-20 (or part of it) for exiles.

outline: The heading: Zephaniah, in Josiah's days
The sweep: everything off the surface of the ground
Judah's idols, officials and complacent merchants
The great day of the LORD
Seek the LORD, you humble of the land
Against Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush, and Assyria with Nineveh
Woe to the rebellious and defiled city
Wait for me: pure lips for the peoples and a humble remnant
The shout of joy of Daughter Zion and the LORD's own joy

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Zephaniah in the reign of Josiah (640 to 609 BC), the idolatry Josiah purged, the fall of Nineveh in 612, the Philistine cities, the Babylonian conquest of Judah in 597 and 586, and the view that the Scythians were the invader (a conjecture based on Herodotus).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Authorship and unity, the date before or after 622, the post-exilic additions (2:8-11 and 3:9-20), the frame of 1:2-3 and 1:18, the Hebrew text of the hard verses (2:1-2; 2:14; 3:1; 3:8; 3:17-18) and the Greek differences.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Zephaniah as one of the Twelve in a single scroll (Bava Batra 14b-15a) and the Talmud's use of 1:12 in the search for leaven (Pesachim 7b-8a). This lens is thin here: no Targum or medieval passage is quoted.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The Dies irae and the church's reading of the day as the last judgment, Jerome on 3:8 and the resurrection, Pentecost and 3:9, the Beatitudes and 3:12, and the Annunciation and 3:14-17, all labeled as the church's reading.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: The sweep of the whole earth (1:2-3; 1:18; 3:8), the day of the LORD, the nations' worship (2:11; 3:9) and the gathered remnant (3:12-20) as the end of the age: dispensationalist, amillennial, Catholic and Orthodox, and Jewish readings.

sections.b:
Read it aloud and in order. The book is built from short, hammering lines and from sounds that return: asaf ("gather"), gibbor ("warrior"), teru'ah ("battle cry" and "shout of joy"), qerev ("in your midst"), bosheth ("shame"), 'alaz ("exult"). The notes point these out. The prophet names streets and gates so each hearer sees his own place on the list, and he calls on the LORD's own voice in the first person throughout. He does not say who the invader is; the reader must listen for it.

Hear the book's three movements. Chapter 1 is judgment: Judah and the whole earth. Chapter 2 opens with a call to the humble and then turns around the compass to the nations. Chapter 3 begins with Jerusalem's guilt and ends with the nations' pure lips, a humble remnant and the LORD's own ringing cry of joy.

Zephaniah 1:7-18 is the fullest single description of the day of the LORD in the Twelve. Amos 5:18-20 first said that the day, which the people hoped would be light, is darkness. Isaiah 2 and 13, Joel 1-3, Obadiah and Ezekiel 30 followed. Zephaniah gathers the images: the sacrifice with its invited guests (compare Isaiah 34:6), the search with lamps, the warrior's cry, the ram's horn, darkness at midday, silver and gold that cannot rescue. Whether it means the Babylonian conquest, the last judgment or both is the main question of the book; the notes and the card on 1:14-18 show the readings. See the topic page.

The heading dates the book to Josiah's reign. Read 2 Kings 22-23 and 2 Chronicles 34-35 beside it. The sins Zephaniah names (Baal, the idol priests, the host of heaven, Milcom, the roof altars) are the shrines Josiah removed. Huldah, the woman prophet whom Josiah's officials consulted, lived in the Second District of Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14), which Zephaniah names in 1:10. Jeremiah began to prophesy in the same reign (Jeremiah 1:2). Nahum and Habakkuk, the books before Zephaniah in the Twelve, speak to the fall of Nineveh and the rise of Babylon.

In the 1800s and early 1900s many scholars said that the invader Zephaniah and Jeremiah feared was the Scythians, nomad horsemen whom Herodotus says swept through western Asia (Histories 1.103-106). Herodotus says the Scythians plundered the temple of the goddess at Ashkelon, which is why the theory arose, since Zephaniah 2:4 is about Ashkelon. The book never names the invader, no other source mentions a Scythian attack on Judah, and most recent commentators think it was Babylon, or that the prophet chose not to say. The theory is a view, not a fact.

sections.h: The Hebrew text, the Greek and the scrolls
sections.b: The Plain translates the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex. The Greek (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus) is an older translation, not the later revision of the Twelve toward the Hebrew (the "kaige" revision found in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever), and it differs from the Hebrew at 1:3, 1:4, 1:9, 1:10, 2:1, 2:2, 2:6, 2:9, 2:14, 3:1, 3:3, 3:7, 3:9, 3:10, 3:15, 3:17 and 3:18. Four scrolls from the Judean desert preserve parts of the Hebrew: 4QXII-b (4Q77), 4QXII-c (4Q78) and 4QXII-g (4Q82) from Qumran Cave 4, and Mur88 from Murabba'at. Mur88, from the early 100s AD, preserves most of 1:11 to 3:20 and agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling and a few small differences noted in the variants. The Plain follows the Hebrew everywhere; where the Greek differs and the difference matters, the variants show it. Verses 1:3-10 and 3:7 are not preserved in any scroll. These are the only four scrolls the transcription used by this site (Abegg, Bowley and Cook) shows for Zephaniah. The Greek revision scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) and the fragmentary commentaries (pesharim) from Qumran that touch Zephaniah are not examined here. Smaller Greek differences (for example at 1:7, 1:11, 2:5, 2:11, 3:6, 3:10 and 3:12) are given in the notes on those verses, not as variant entries.

sections.h: The Dies irae and the church's reading
sections.b: The Latin Bible (Jerome's Vulgate) renders Zephaniah 1:15 as dies irae, dies illa, "a day of wrath, that day." Those words open the medieval Latin hymn of the funeral Mass, the Dies irae, which pictures the last judgment. It is usually attributed to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan of the 1200s, though the attribution is uncertain. Composers including Mozart and Verdi set it. The 1969 reform of the funeral rite removed it as the Requiem sequence; the 1962 Missal keeps it, and the Liturgy of the Hours uses it divided into three hymns. The hymn is the church's reading of the day as the last day; Zephaniah's own words say "the day of the LORD" without saying that it is the end of the world. See the topic page.

The Hebrew Bible counts Zephaniah among the Twelve, one scroll (Bava Batra 14b-15a). The Talmud cites 1:12 ("I will search Jerusalem with lamps") in discussing why the search for leaven before Passover is done by lamp (Bavli Pesachim 7b-8a). In the Hebrew order Zephaniah stands between Habakkuk and Haggai, which gives its pairing with Habakkuk's "Hush before him, all the earth" (Habakkuk 2:20) and Zephaniah's "Hush before the Lord GOD" (1:7) a place in the scroll's design.

This lens is thin in this book. The Targum Jonathan translates the book into Aramaic and medieval Jewish commentators wrote on it, but no passage of the Targum or of those commentators is quoted here, and Jewish readings of 3:9 ("pure lips") are not documented.

spec.title: One verb frames the book
spec.body: The Hebrew verb 'asaf means both "gather in" and "sweep away" and opens the book twice (1:2-3). It returns when the LORD gathers the nations for judgment (3:8) and, in a sibling verb, when he gathers the lame and the outcast (3:18-20). My suggestion is that Zephaniah is built so that the same action, the LORD's gathering, is first the end of everything and then the rescue of the scattered. This is Claude's observation, not a settled view; it overlaps with commentators who note the pun in 1:2.

spec.title: The sounds come back
spec.body: Four Hebrew sounds in chapter 1 return, turned, in chapter 3: the battle cry (teru'ah, 1:16) becomes the shout of joy (hari'u, 3:14); the warrior (gibbor) who cries out in defeat (1:14) is the warrior who rescues (3:17); the wrongdoer who has no shame (3:5) becomes the people whose shame the LORD turns into praise (3:19); the proud who exult (2:15; 3:11) are replaced by the humble who are told to exult (3:14). This is my reading of the book's design; commentators note several of the pairs but I have not seen all four set out together.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll image in the style of ancient manuscript, cave drawing and modern art with soft, torn edges: a great wind sweeping birds, fish, animals and people off a strip of ground, drawn as simple cave-painting figures in ochre and charcoal, with the faint outline of a flood behind. No hard rectangle border.

Sketched on old parchment with soft edges: a dark Jerusalem of flat roofs and narrow alleys at night, a hand holding up a small clay lamp to light a hidden corner, men crouched on rooftops facing the stars. Ink and wash, hieroglyph-like marks along the edge, no square frame.

An ancient-manuscript and modern-art style image with torn, soft edges: a woman, Daughter Zion, standing in a quiet crowd of humble and limping people, and above and around her a warm light shaped like an open mouth crying out for joy, drawn in gold and blue ink on aged paper, no hard border.
